articles.title: Venezuelan opposition leader returns after 10 months in exile
articles.summary: [Reuters] Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile. "I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail. In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro. The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US. Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands. Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González, confirmed her arrival, writing in a statement: "I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil." "Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" González said. He added that he will soon join Machado in Venezuela to advance the country "toward freedom". An advisor to Machado said in September that over the previous few weeks Machado had attempted seven times to return to Venezuela, but was denied each time. There have been reports that the US was involved in delaying her return, which it has denied. It's unclear what Machado plans to do next now that she's back, but she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held . Her ability to return to her country was always contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now been granted. [Reuters] A staunch supporter of democracy, Machado won an independent presidential primary election - held outside the Maduro government's official election authority - in 2023, earning more than 90% of the vote. Despite winning the primary, Maduro's government barred Machado from running for office, accusing her of fraud and tax violations. Machado denied the allegations, calling them politically motivated. She spent her final days in the country hiding in safehouses before her fleeing to Norway to accept the Nobel Prize. In the 2024 election, Machado's ally González ran in her place against Maduro. The electoral authority, which is closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public. The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence. Maduro was removed from the country by US forces in January, and is currently jailed in New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges. He has pleaded not guilty. A spokesman for Machado called her return "a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future". "We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the US Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support," her spokesperson, David Smolansky, added. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said, "I don't know anything about" her return, and added that he hoped she was "safe". "I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe," he said. In January, Machado visited the White House and gifted her Nobel prize award to Trump . The committee that issues the prize had said "it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised his country's role in securing her return through political reconciliation talks. "The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms Machado to Venezuela is the direct result of the US supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile," he posted on X. He added: "We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy." articles.title: 12 people shot, including children, after Florida A&M homecoming game
articles.summary: At least 12 people were injured, including six children, amid a Saturday evening shooting in Tallahassee, near the campus of Florida A&M University, officials said. Eleven of those who were injured had gunshot wounds, Tallahassee Chief of Police Lawrence Revell told reporters during a late-night press conference. "Six are adults and six are juveniles," he said. "We know our youngest victim is 11 years old. At least three of our victims have sustained serious injuries and one of those is in critical condition. Eight of those are reported to be in stable condition." WTXL - PHOTO: Police investigate a shooting near the campus of Florida A&M University, October 24, 2026, that left 12 people injured. The person who was injured but not from a gunshot was "a grandmother of one of the victims," the chief said, adding that she "injured herself fleeing from the scene." In an update Sunday morning, the Tallahassee Police Department (TPD) said that six of the victims remain hospitalized, one of whom is in critical condition. Five other victims have been released from the hospital, police said. No arrests had been announced as of Sunday morning. Police said they are working to identify those responsible for the shooting and sought the public's help, asking anyone with information about the shooting to contact investigators immediately. Police also asked that anyone with photos or video share them with investigators. "We will determine what happened, identify those responsible, and get answers for all of the victims, their families and everyone impacted by this tragedy,” Revell said in a statement released on Sunday. “We know there are people who saw something, heard something or may have video that could help us piece together exactly what happened. WTXL - PHOTO: Police crime scene tape at the scene of a shooting, October 24, 2026, near the campus of Florida A&M University that left 12 people injured. "We need our community's help. No detail is too small, and no piece of information should go unreported," Revell added. "If you know something, please share it with our detectives. Your information could be the key to holding those responsible accountable." Police described the shooting as an "altercation [that] occurred between individuals" near the intersection of Perry and Manatee streets, which is just outside Florida A&M University's Bragg Memorial Stadium. "The University is aware of an incident that occurred near campus on Perry Street on the evening of October 24," the school said in a statement. "The Tallahassee Police Department is on the scene and actively investigating the situation." articles.title: LIV Golf faces a make-or-break deadline — and only 4 players have signed on
articles.summary: Dustin Johnson and other players are considering whether to continue with LIV Golf. ASSOCIATED PRESS One way or another, LIV Golf is in its final days as originally created. The tour began life as a PGA Tour breakaway funded by Saudi Arabia's virtually limitless Public Investment Fund, but now is working to both line up financing and hold onto players in preparation for what league officials have termed "LIV 2.0." With a self-imposed go/no-go deadline nearing, several recent developments have complicated plans for a new version of the league. For players, LIV's chief drawing card was the paychecks with astounding numbers of zeroes. Stars, former stars and non-stars alike all cashed in during LIV's run, earning many millions more than they would have been able to on the PGA Tour or the Europe-based DP World Tour. But when Saudi Arabia cut off funding for LIV in April, the pipeline for those paychecks dried up, and now player after player has decided to take their chances elsewhere. The most notable defection came several weeks ago, when Jon Rahm decided he'd had enough of LIV. Rahm's jump to LIV in late 2023 was a seismic moment in golf history, a declaration that the league was capable of enticing even one of the world's best players. But after three years of absolute domination on LIV and underperformance in majors, Rahm opted to walk away from millions — perhaps even tens of millions — owed to him under his initial contract. Rahm's future plans aren't yet known, but the fact that he was willing to forgo the remainder of his contract is a stark statement on his belief in LIV 2.0. Several other notable players have followed Rahm out the door. In recent days, Ian Poulter announced he would be ending his LIV tenure, expressing gratitude on X for the opportunity: Life update…✍🏼 pic.twitter.com/kdSQIOmxZ0 — Ian Poulter (@IanJamesPoulter) October 23, 2026 Rahm's Legion XIII teammate Tyrrell Hatton also announced he wouldn't be playing in LIV 2.0. Like Rahm, his next event will be the DP World Tour's Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship in early November. Major winners Sergio Garcia and Louis Oosthuizen, among many others, have declared that they intend to pursue other opportunities outside LIV Golf. The defection of so many notable players — in name if not necessarily in current skill — makes the challenge of bringing LIV Golf 2.0 to light that much more difficult. Professional golf on an international scale is a star-driven system, and having notable names in the field is the fastest way to draw attention to an event. Accordingly, LIV's new investor, BC Partners Credit, had set a deadline of Sunday, Oct. 25, for players to commit to the league, though BC has the ability to move that deadline. LIV's own attorneys have suggested in recent bankruptcy hearings that the league would make a decision on its future existence by the end of this month. Several players aren't simply walking away from LIV, however; they're seeking what they claim they're still owed. On Sunday, The Athletic r eported that more than 10 players , led by Masters champions Dustin Johnson and Bubba Watson, are seeking more favorable severance deals from the Public Investment Fund. The unpaid terms of their contracts reportedly total more than $100 million. Johnson's attorney David Cornwell suggested that the players are reluctant to sign on with LIV 2.0 until the remaining obligations of LIV 1.0 reach a satisfactory conclusion. The Athletic reported that the PIF had offered the players two cents on the dollar for the remainder of those contracts, and Cornwell indicated that the PIF's decision to cut off funding for LIV ought to give other sports entities pause. "The PIF was an honorable business partner until what we regard as its abandonment of LIV golfers," Cornwell told The Athletic. "Professional sports leagues and their player unions in the United States, along with sports organizations worldwide, should take notice: the PIF's treatment of LIV golfers may signal how it will treat professional athletes in other sports. How you do one thing is usually how you do everything." At the same time, court documents indicated that many LIV executives were paid hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars in retention payments and bonuses prior to the league's bankruptcy filing this summer. While retention payments aren't uncommon during bankruptcy proceedings, the fact that LIV was paying significant amounts to executives while vendors went unpaid raised questions and opened up the league to external criticism. LIV and BC Partners have developed a plan that could bring in up to $300 million in financing for LIV 2.0, and players would hold a majority ownership stake in the new entity. However, as of the deadline date of Sunday only four players — Richard Bland, Ben Campbell, Brendan Steele and Cameron Tringale — had formally committed to the next iteration of the league. Bryson DeChambeau, a free agent who has been linked to the LIV restructuring in the last few months, has not formally committed to the next version of the league just yet. articles.title: A strange twist in Alaska's Senate race has Trump's DOJ fighting to block results
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Justice Department's newly filed lawsuit to prevent Alaska state officials from certifying election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses in November. In an at-times contentious interview with CNN’s “State of the Union,” Blanche pointed out that according to the Constitution, Congress can create laws at any time to regulate elections. But when host Dana Bash asked what crime the administration was arguing was being committed, Blanche replied, “It depends.” “There could be a crime,” said Blanche. “But the real wrong here is that Alaskans are going to be confused and will not have their vote heard. So an Alaskan intends to vote for one candidate, but is confused because of a second candidate with exactly the same name who has voted Democrat his entire life, who donated money to the other Democrat opponent, is running.” Bash pressed Blanche on how it is illegal for two candidates with the same name to be on a ballot at the same time. "It is an obligation of the states to avoid confusion, among other things, confusion in the minds of voters in the election process,” Blanche replied. “So the question is whether Alaska, by allowing this to happen, is violating the law and the federal law and the constitution by allowing confusion in the ballot." The Alaskan Supreme Court in June ruled that both Sullivans may remain on the ballot as the incumbent faces off in a tight reelection battle with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. The four-person Senate ranked-choice ballot for the general election specifies that Dan S. Sullivan is a "Registered Republican" and the "incumbent" — no information is listed after Dan J. Sullivan Jr's name. Regardless, in the suit filed Thursday , DOJ argued that Dan J. Sullivan Jr.’s name on the ballot constitutes a purposeful effort to mislead voters. Still, it’s unclear how much the court can do about the Justice Department’s lawsuit. With ballots secret, it is virtually impossible for the Justice Department to identify specific voters and clarify which Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for. Blanche, though, seemed unconcerned about that hurdle. “There are a number of scenarios where it could be obvious that a voter was confused by the way they wrote down candidates,” said Blanche. Republican groups have worked to differentiate between the two Sullivans . President Donald Trump on Friday said the legal challenge was his idea, though Blanche on Sunday declined to state whether the president had directed him to file the suit. "I will never talk about any communications I have with the president of the United States,” he said. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who is not up for reelection this year, said Friday that the lawsuit is unnecessary. “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” Murkowski said in a post on X . “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.” Her comments drew the ire of Trump, who on Saturday called Murkowski “Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far,” in a post to Truth Social . Trump said that Alaska’s ranked choice voting system is “a TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter, so that Senator Dan Sullivan will lose Votes to a man who has never participated in Politics before, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.” “He is only there because the Democrats want to steal the Election, and Murkowski probably wants that to happen, which is why she is against the DOJ filing a Lawsuit in order to stop this impending crime and tragedy,” Trump added. “I have delivered for Alaska at Historic Levels, nobody has ever seen anything like it, and all I’m asking for is a FAIR AND HONEST SENATORIAL ELECTION! Lisa Murkowski is a DISGRACE to Alaska and our Country. You just don’t get any worse!" Democratic leaders have also widely condemned the lawsuit, arguing the president is attempting to lay the foundation to overturn the midterm election results if their candidates win critical elections — something Bash asked Blanche about on Sunday. “One of the big questions is whether or not the president is laying the groundwork for a scenario where, whether it's Alaska or somewhere else, there is, in your words a couple of days ago, a 'doomsday scenario' and we could be in a situation where President Trump tries to overturn the election and the result of that could be, god forbid, what we saw after January 6th,” Bash said. Blanche quickly fired back: “Oh stop it. You gotta stop it with that. You're not being a real person. You set me up. You're saying, “'Mr. Attorney General, because the president of the United States wants to stop fraud and confusion in Alaska, is he going to do something crazy?' That is not a real question.” Bash replied that she did not think it was an unfair question, but Blanche argued that the premise of the question was untrue. “Instead of focusing on how we can address that and how we can remedy that, you're talking about January 6th,” he said. “That's so embarrassing to this network that that's what you're talking about.” “Oh, come on,” Bash said. "Don't “oh, come on” me,” replied Blanche. “There's literally confusion." It wasn’t the only tense interview Blanche had Sunday. In an appearance on CBS’ “Face the Nation,” Blanche accused host Margaret Brennan of lying over the wording of the Justice Department’s lawsuit . “The Alaska Supreme Court did take on this matter,” Brennan began, referring to the court’s June decision. “No, they didn't. That's a state law,” interrupted Blanche. “In this country, the states administer the elections. This is how the state came up with the issue and how to handle any confusion,” Brennan said as the Alaskan ballot was shown on the screen. “You’re not telling the truth,” said Blanche. Brennan asked why identifying Sullivan as the incumbent is insufficient for the administration. “Well, listen, I don't know if it's sufficient,” said Blanche. “But I can tell you this: that the director of the Alaska election system has said that it will likely cause confusion.” Brennan pointed out that the ballots are already circulating, and voting may already be underway, as many vote by mail in Alaska. She then pressed Blanche on Trump claiming responsibility for the lawsuit, to which Blanche reiterated that he will not share his communications with the president. “The president of the United States said this on camera ,” Brennan replied. “He said, "I told them to do it." Did he tell that to you?” “He didn’t say that on camera,” argued Blanche, before adding Trump had been looking at the situation for “months and months and months.” He later added that he had “no idea” who Trump was referring to, and even if he did, he would “most certainly not” talk about it. Brennan then pivoted to read several lines from DOJ’s lawsuit, including that the suit defined voter confusion as Sen. Sullivan not winning the election and that had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast for the incumbent then he would have won. As she spoke, Blanche interrupted again. “That’s not what it says,” he said. “I’m quoting from it,” Brennan replied, holding up a printed version of the suit. “You are telling them not to certify it. What right does the federal government have telling a state not to certify or how to certify?” After a moment of crosstalk, Blanche stated: "If you talk the whole time you're not going to get answers out of me. If you let me answer your question I can address your question." He then said the suit does not call for officials to avoid certifying the election. “All we're doing is trying to put guardrails in place so that if that happens there's a system allowed where the ballots are kept in a way so we can determine whether there was confusion,” he explained. In his interview with CNN, Blanche denied any political motivations were behind the Justice Department’s lawsuit. “It's important the American people understand that we are not — President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape or form,” he said. “What we're trying to do is make it clear that if it is obvious after the election, that confusion led to an improper and illegal result that the Alaskan system should be able to address that.” In an interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday, Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) argued the administration has no standing to bring the Alaska lawsuit, and he lambasted Blanche for leading a “disgraceful campaign.” “This suit has no chance of succeeding,” said Schiff. “But the fact that Todd Blanche and the Justice Department are willing to go along with it, they're willing to put their name on it, is an indication of how far they will go after this election is over to try to challenge the results.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/25/blanche-alaska-lawsuit-could-be-crime-01134861

articles.title: ICE said a man jumped on the hood of their vehicle. Video — and police — say otherwise.
articles.summary: A Northern California man was responding to a call about ICE activity in his city when surveillance footage showed he was hit by an agent in an SUV on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. - Obtained by CNN When footage of a man being hit by federal immigration officers’ SUV in Northern California became public, the Department of Homeland Security responded by saying the man had jumped on the vehicle’s hood. Local police raised doubts about federal officials’ account as they announced a criminal investigation into Tuesday morning’s incident involving the pedestrian, 37-year-old Antonio Moreida, citing video footage that contradicted DHS’ statement. Footage from a nearby surveillance camera, a bystander’s cellphone recording and Moreida’s GoPro, which had already been made public at the time of the agency’s statement, told a different story of what happened on a residential street in Woodland, an agricultural city just outside of Sacramento. The incident is the latest in which DHS’ account has been contradicted by officials and video evidence amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Police contradict ICE account In a statement Wednesday morning, DHS said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers didn’t hit a pedestrian. “An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement in response to CNN’s request for information. “The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department. Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation,” apparently accusing the man of faking his injuries. After the incident on Tuesday, Woodland Police Chief Ryan Kinnan said in a statement he found footage of the incident troubling. Investigators were working to gather evidence and statements and to review available audio and video related to the incident, including video taken from multiple perspectives, police said in a Facebook post . Woodland Police didn’t take part in the ICE operation the agents were involved in that morning, police said. The following day, Woodland Police called DHS’ account “inconsistent.” “Certain claims made in the DHS statement are inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed by Woodland Police investigators,” Kinnan said in an update Wednesday . The update said investigators had established, based on video evidence, the pedestrian had been hit by the vehicle driven by ICE agents and that he had not jumped onto the vehicle. The local police department is conducting a criminal investigation into the events leading up to the collision and the actions of those involved, Kinnan said Wednesday. By Thursday, in response to follow-up questions about the video footage, federal officials no longer said the person jumped on the hood. “This individual chose to directly impede a law enforcement action and stand in the middle of an active road,” an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. “Our officers deliberately attempted to avoid making contact with this anti-ice protestor and drive around him, while also braking. We strongly urge individuals to not stand in the middle of active roadways while a law enforcement vehicle is approaching.” What footage shows Footage reviewed by CNN shows Moreida, a Woodland resident, in the middle of the street at around 9:40 a.m. Tuesday. Moreida said he had responded to a call that morning by NorCal Resist, a group which monitors immigration operations, about ICE activity in Woodland, he told CNN on Tuesday, hours after the incident. unknown content item - He said he was trying to record agents’ unmarked vehicles. He had been recording one vehicle, standing on the car’s driver’s side, when it turned left and drove off, which he said pushed him into the middle of the street. Video from Moreida’s GoPro shows him following a black Dodge Durango with tinted windows as it drives down the street. Then, he said he heard a loud engine before seeing the agents’ black Chevy Tahoe drive toward him, which is shown in his GoPro footage, though the video has no audio. unknown content item - Down the street, the bystander’s cellphone video shows the Durango pass the Tahoe, which has tinted windows, on a residential street. In the video’s background, people can be heard blowing whistles, presumably to alert people nearby of ICE’s presence in the neighborhood. The ICE agent driving the Tahoe moves toward Moreida and between the cars with its brake lights on, footage shows. In the bystander’s video, Moreida isn’t yet visible. The SUV’s wheels begin to turn to the left only a few feet from Moreida, a wider angle of surveillance footage from a home shows. unknown content item - “The individual was standing in the street long enough that a reasonable person should be able to see them and recognize that they were there,” said Ryan Schwank , a former ICE attorney and training instructor who reviewed the videos provided by CNN. Schwank also took issue with ICE’s characterization that Moreida was standing in the middle of an active road and impeding law enforcement’s actions. “When we’re looking at Antonio’s actions, he’s not impeding. He’s not standing blocking the vehicle from moving,” he said. “He’s standing and filming, and that’s well within his bounds to do. He’s well within his rights to do what he was doing.” Moreida’s GoPro appears to show when he’s struck by the front-right side of the vehicle before he drops his camera. “Before I knew it, it just drove straight into me,” he said. “I took the hood of the car straight to the chest. It initially took the wind out of me and I couldn’t breathe.” The surveillance footage shows Moreida take a step back when he appears to make contact with the car. He is then seen falling toward the ground, off the front-right side of the car, the footage shows. A bystander's cellphone video shows the moments when an SUV driven by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer hit a man filming federal immigration enforcement operations in Woodland, California, on October 20, 2026. -  NorCal Resist In the bystander’s footage from behind, a screeching noise is heard before the Tahoe jolts forward. The SUV veers left before straightening out, the video shows. The bystander’s angle shows the Tahoe brake lights turn off. Moreida is then visible in the bystander’s video, falling to the ground and rolling, first on his back with his legs swinging above him. He then appears seated upright in the nearby surveillance footage, this time facing the sidewalk. The SUV’s brake lights turn back on briefly before it drives farther down the street, the surveillance footage shows. The driver, an ICE agent, stayed near the scene and called local dispatch, Woodland Police said. The agent cooperated with police during the initial investigation, the local agency said. Moreida said an off-duty EMT provided him aid at the scene before Woodland Police officers arrived. Federal agents didn’t approach him after he was hit by the SUV, he said. Moreida said he was eventually transported to the hospital. He said he had X-rays taken of his swollen knees, where he said he had the most damage. In addition, he said he has bruises and cuts from the road. ICE has reduced the amount of training for officers, including in vehicle operations and how to deal with confrontations, said Schwank, who is now an agency whistleblower after resigning in February . On Saturday, ICE said it is instituting additional training for officers. “ICE training will now be extending to 72 days. The change, effective June 2, 2026, will apply to all new academy classes beginning July 1, 2026. All graduates of the previous academy curriculum will attend follow-on training at the Advanced Field Officer Training Program,” an ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CNN. “As we have said all along, ICE training does not end when recruits graduate from the academy. ICE officers go through a rigorous on-the-job training and mentorship. This additional training is tracked online and monitored closely.” Local officials call for investigations Soon after it became public, local officials expressed dismay over the incident, which occurred in a rural Northern California community that’s about half Latino. More than a fifth of the population is foreign-born, according to US Census estimates . “The lack of truth in the Department of Homeland Security’s statement is evidenced by video taken at the scene,” Woodland Mayor Tom Stallard said in a statement issued Wednesday. “All of us can be assured that the Police Department’s investigation into this disturbing incident will continue to be speedy, fair, and impartial.” US Rep. Mike Thompson, a Democrat whose district includes Woodland, said ICE’s statements about the facts surrounding the incident were disappointing but not surprising. “ICE has a history of trying to hide the facts and mislead the public,” he told CNN. “And this is another example of that happening.” On the day of the operation, Thompson called on Acting ICE Director David Venturella to investigate the collision, including by preserving evidence and cooperating with local authorities. As of Friday, the congressman had yet to receive a response to his letter, his office told CNN. CNN’s Taylor Galgano contributed to this report. articles.title: Poll finds Democrats still boosted by voters' economic concerns
articles.summary: Call it the "avoidance" election , with many on each side more motivated by trying to prevent or stop things than by what they'll gain. Against a backdrop of continued concern about inflation and the economy , Democrats maintain their lead in a bid for a House majority . They're currently on pace for 229 seats in our CBS News House model estimate, which translates voters' congressional preferences into seats. The potential range of outcomes could reach into the 230s in our model, but Republicans do still have a very narrow path to hold the majority, too. While that Democratic lead has been durable over recent weeks, it hasn't expanded, either. In other words, there isn't a growing wave, at least not as of today. If anything, the still undecided or uncertain voters tend to profile as more Republican. Whether they decide to show up is perhaps the key question of 2026. Either way, voters describe a dynamic in which they're more motivated in opposition to things they think might happen. For instance: More think gas prices will go up if Republicans win than if Democrats do. (Though they don't think Democrats will make gas prices go down.) Most voters don't think Democrats have a plan and won't make people financially better off, either...But more voters think they'll be worse off if Republicans win. The president remains a central factor. It would be a high number voting either to support or oppose a president in a midterm if this sentiment holds through Election Day. Most of the Democrats' voters are trying to oppose either President Trump or Republicans, even more than to help Democrats. (Whether that rationale ultimately limits Democrats' gains or not is another key question.) But he's motivating for most Republicans, especially MAGA. Some of this lead is attributed to more Democrats saying they'll either definitely vote, or have already voted early. But this is not over: The voters who describe themselves as only "probably" or "maybe" going to vote are more Republican. If they become motivated, this can all change. So, what happens if either party wins? Few voters think gas prices will go down no matter who wins. But the GOP is now relatively more associated in voters' minds with rising gas prices: More think they'll go up if Republicans win than if Democrats do. Most voters don't think they'll be better off financially, no matter who wins. That cynicism does permeate the electorate. But as a choice, relatively more think they'll do better with Democrats. Most voters think there will be more corruption in government if Republicans maintain control of Congress. Both Democrats and Republicans — at about similar large majorities — see government corruption as a factor in their votes. The Trump factor: A motivator for both sides, but more so for Democrats Mr. Trump looms large over the midterms, particularly for Democrats. More than seven in 10 voting for Democrats say their vote for Congress is to oppose him. Mr. Trump is also a factor for those backing Republicans. Most say their vote is to support him, but to a lesser extent than Democrats are voting to oppose him. For most who are backing Democrats, their motivation is more about stopping Mr. Trump and GOP policies than advancing the Democrats' own policies. Here's how prevalent opposition to either party is as a motivating force this year. Neither Democrats nor Republicans are perceived by a majority of voters as having a clear plan, should either win control of Congress. There are four in 10 voters supporting Democrats who don't believe the party has a clear plan, should they win. They say opposition to Mr. Trump is the main motivator for them. Meanwhile, there are four in 10 voting Republican who say their vote isn't about the president. They're less likely to consider themselves MAGA, tend to just "somewhat," rather than "strongly," approve of Mr. Trump. But a big majority of them have an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party – so they remain in the Republican camp. Other issues Many voters feel a win by the other side is a threat to their way of life. Democrats think a Republican win would be a threat to theirs. MAGA Republicans in particular, more so than non-MAGA, think the Democrats would be a threat. Although the issue ranks behind others as a factor in voters' decisions, Republicans lead Democrats among those who consider transgender issues a major factor in their vote. Immigration There are a third of voters who think the Democratic Party puts the interests of recent immigrants ahead of those of U.S. citizens, and voters who hold this view are backing Republicans in big numbers. (Another third does think the Democratic Party prioritizes both groups, and these voters are supporting Democrats.) Trump and finances Americans' overall ratings of the economy continue to be negative, as they have been for years. They've even dipped a bit lower now, to where they were last spring. And most likely voters feel the president's policies are making them financially worse off. The economy and inflation remain top concerns. Those calling inflation a very important issue mostly back Democrats, as do those who feel prices have been difficult or a hardship. Against that backdrop, voters voice broader concern about whose financial interests they think the president prioritizes. More feel he prioritizes his own financial interests and those of his family over the financial interests of the people in the country. And those who hold this view are backing Democrats. Republicans mostly feel Mr. Trump prioritizes the financial interests of people in the country over his own. Trump on the trail: Is he helping or hurting? The president's numerous appearances on the campaign trail may help to rally the base behind Republican candidates, but those events may not have as much impact with the rest of the party. Most MAGA Republicans say that when they see Trump campaigning for political candidates, it makes them more likely to vote for Republicans. For many non-MAGA Republicans, these campaign events do not do that. The voting process Most voters express at least some confidence in their own local and county elections administration to conduct the election process, including determining eligibility and correctly counting ballots. In turn, most tend to voice confidence that their own vote will be recorded and counted accurately in this election. On both of these measures, more Democrats than Republicans are very confident. Republicans are far more likely to believe that illegal voting by non-citizens happens in federal elections. This CBS News/YouGov survey was conducted with a nationally representative sample of 2,355 U.S. adults interviewed between October 21-23, 2026. The sample was weighted to be representative of adults nationwide according to gender, age, race, and education, based on the U.S. Census American Community Survey and Current Population Survey, as well as 2024 presidential vote. The margin of error for the total sample is ±2.6 points, it is ± 2.9  points for the sample of registered voters, and  ± 3.0 points for likely voters. The estimated numbers of Republican and Democratic seats come from a statistical model developed by CBS News and YouGov which includes data from this poll, past vote and other district-level characteristics, demographics and historical patterns. These estimates are subject to statistical error. We simulate many elections, with the error calibrated to include historical polling accuracy, to obtain a range of seat estimates. We report 95% confidence intervals from the simulations. These estimates describe which party is ahead today and may change as additional data are collected closer to the election. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/poll-house-estimate-midterm-elections-2026/

articles.title: She blocked his bid to become a federal judge. Now he's running for her Senate seat.
articles.summary: Why are major Democrats and Republicans flocking to Mississippi in recent weeks? In a climate where polls show President Donald Trump's approval ratings cratering, Democrats are unusually optimistic about Scott Colom's chances of flipping the Senate seat held by incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith -- even in deep-red Mississippi. "We got to have a senator that looks out for Mississippi, that puts Mississippi farmers first, Mississippi small businesses first, represent our values by not allowing corruption to ruin our country and actually delivers on the commitments to put America first," Colom told ABC News in an interview earlier this week. Sarah Warnock/AP Photo - PHOTO: Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks during a voting rights town hall at the historic Farish Street Baptist Church in Jackson, Miss., Aug. 1, 2026. The incumbent's campaign dismisses the Democratic push as the last-ditch effort of a campaign that will fall short. Gov. Wes Moore says key races in South 'in play,' Democrats 'made mistakes' not investing earlier Colom is a district attorney for four counties along the Mississippi-Alabama border and a former nominee to become a U.S. district judge. He would be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction. Democrats have argued that Colom's prominent credentials, as well as voter pushback against Republican incumbents and motivation among Democratic-leaning Black voters, could help boost him. Mississippi's population is around 36% Black, according to U.S. Census data . Colom faces an uphill battle, as Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982 and voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by around 20 points. ABC News rates the race solid Republican. But he has gotten the attention of national Democrats; major party figures such as former former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock have campaigned with him. Former President Barack Obama also recorded an ad for him released earlier this month. Harris, during a rally with Colom on Thursday, told attendees, "I've been in those rooms where there's no cameras, it's senators talking to each other... When you have a voice like his in that room, just think about the impact that's going to have on the decisions coming out of that room. Think about that. This is no ordinary time, and this is no ordinary man." AP Photo - PHOTO: Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigns for candidate Scott Colom in Mississippi, Oct. 22, 2026. Colom also went viral online last week after a social video he posted showed Hyde-Smith, during a local news interview from February, saying "You have so many proteins to choose from" while discussing how to deal with higher prices on meat and other goods. In the interview, Hyde-Smith also spoke about working on regulations that would help energy production, and tax incentives to help development. But it was the proteins part that Colom's campaign seized on, with a punchy video that featured voters mocking the senator's words, with one saying, "Pick another protein ... I'd rather pick another Senator instead." (The campaign has confirmed to ABC News that the video has been turned into a campaign ad.) Sarah Warnock/AP Photo - PHOTO: Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom listens during a maternal health roundtable at the Capital Club in Jackson, Miss., Aug. 1, 2026. One concrete sign of confidence among Democrats over Colom's chances came on Tuesday, when the Senate Majority PAC, an outside group aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on an ad campaign across broadcast TV and digital for ads for Colom. Asked what signs the group sees in Mississippi that makes it worth investing in, spokesperson Lauren French wrote, "Cindy Hyde-Smith has spent a decade in Washington without passing a single piece of legislation, and Mississippians have noticed." Hyde-Smith has cosponsored legislation that has passed into law but legislation she initially sponsored or reintroduced has not become law, according to congressional records . Asked to respond to Senate Majority PAC, Hyde-Smith's campaign pointed to how bills from lawmakers "are often passed as part of larger legislative packages," and that has been true for some of Hyde-Smith's bills, including the first one she introduced. The campaign also pointed out that she is running for only her second full term. French said Colom is running a "disciplined campaign" with messages resonating with voters. Colom and Hyde-Smith have some history, as she blocked his nomination for federal judge in 2023. She cited his support for transgender rights and having previously been boosted by a George Soros-linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press . He insists his bid for Senate is not motivated by a desire to get back at her. "It has nothing to do with the run for me ... as a Christian, I forgive her. It's about the people in Mississippi," Colom told ABC News. Hyde-Smith dismissed Colom's chances. Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images - PHOTO: Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith arrives in the U.S. Capitol for the first vote of the week, September 22, 2026. "We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith back to the U.S. Senate on November 3rd. This is simply Washington insiders making a last ditch effort to give life to Scott Colom's failing campaign," campaign manager Jake Monssen told ABC News in a statement. Hyde-Smith's supporters may be more motivated after a boost from President Donald Trump, who's set to hold a rally in Mississippi on Monday as part of a swing of campaign rallies mostly in red states. The Republican National Committee announced the rally around a week after Colom's social video went viral, although Trump and the group have not indicated why they are doing the rally there and Trump has expressed confidence in Hyde-Smith. "Cindy Hyde-Smith's very popular ... So if I need to get her over the top, I would go there [to Mississippi]. She's great. Cindy Hyde-Smith is great," Trump told reporters when asked Thursday about the Senate election. Hyde-Smith will be attending the rally, according to her campaign. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/democrats-aim-deep-red-mississippi-senate-seat-scott/story?id=137484924

articles.title: She voted for Trump every time. Then came cancer and the bills.
articles.summary: McALLEN, Texas (AP) — The Ford Expedition rumbled to a stop and Cindy Banda’s bedazzled flip-flops landed on the asphalt of the Houston cancer center’s vast parking lot. She threaded through the rows of cars, a tally of patients who gather here to sit with chemotherapy needles or lie on radiation machines. The elevator dinged open. A year ago in this building, surgeons removed Banda’s right breast, and she still didn't know whether treatment had expunged the cancer from her body. Doctors had told her it would be tough to beat. “I’m more of a positive person myself,” Banda said, now sitting with a white wristband in a dim waiting room. But the bills are harder to dismiss, and the single mother with six children in her care repeated something like a mantra. “Keep the house. Keep the cars. And just keep the kids stable.” That’s true for many Americans, as rising healthcare costs leave more families with a sinking feeling after seeing the bill for surgery or medication. Heading into the Nov. 3 midterm elections, about half of registered voters said healthcare costs are a major problem for them and their families, up from a little more than one-third four years ago, according to a Fox News poll from September. With party control of Congress at stake, registered voters are nearly twice as likely to say they trust Democrats over Republicans to handle healthcare , according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from the same month. Those frustrations, combined with broader concerns over rising prices, have sapped support for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. Banda knows how that feels. She backed Trump in each of his three campaigns, motivated by her opposition to abortion . But when cancer came, the ensuing scramble to make ends meet was painful enough to rearrange her priorities, and she started to think about voting Democratic for the first time. The 46-year-old was ushered into a sterile room for her appointment, her phone lit up with a text. “Please contact TD Auto Finance.” “This one’s $1,300,” she said of the car payment bill. “I have to go back to work.” She had been on sick leave from her job selling internet service for one year, and she needed the income to support her three kids and three more she had taken in after her sister's death. The doctor said her reconstruction surgery could be scheduled early next year. “I was hoping for maybe December,” Banda said, “only because I've met my deductibles.” Come January, she would have to pay down the $7,500 again. Earlier may be possible, the doctor replied, if the skin around her surgical scar loosens. The evening had cooled slightly by the time she walked back through the rows of parked cars, their ebb and flow marking the tide of sickness, survival and death in a small corner of a colossal healthcare industry that saves lives while taking in over $5 trillion every year. Banda paid $8 for parking as she left. Confronting death and debt in America before a midterm election Two weeks later, Banda was back at work, making door-to-door rounds to sell Spectrum's Wi-Fi in McAllen, her city along the U.S.-Mexico border in the Rio Grande Valley. Banda, holding blue flyers, walked along a row of storefronts, some that shuttered since she last was in the area. She hadn't had a sale and commission since October of last year, after the biopsy and diagnosis. The doctor who gave her the news had hugged Banda, and she sobbed even though she never really sobs in front of other people. During chemo, her children took turns buzzing off her wispy hair. When her 9-year-old daughter's hand quivered, a teenage cousin helped guide the clipper over her mother’s scalp. Banda’s first impulse was to maintain normalcy, stability, for the children. But that requires roughly $7,000 a month for utilities, mortgage, car payments and groceries, along with the two water leaks. Then, even with insurance through her job, the surgeries, chemo and radiation added up to over $25,000 that she's been paying off, making Banda one of tens of millions of other people in the United States in medical debt. Banda tries not to dwell on death and debt. “It’ll consume you,” she says. She smothers those thoughts beneath her bubbly demeanor and avoids being alone. But that truce, between her insistence on positivity and the fears that it covers, is brittle. Certain thoughts still arrive uninvited. Banda’s late sister, Melissa, didn’t have life insurance. Banda makes sure it's a payment she never misses. “Sometimes I think, and I shouldn’t think like this, but I’m worth more gone than here,” she said one day. “Obviously, the goal is not that, the goal is to beat it,” she continued, “to keep the house and keep the cars.” So far she has, with the help of others. On top of child support, the father of Banda's 9-year-old often pays $400 a week for a nanny to help with the kids. Banda’s own father sent her $700 before for her recent Houston appointment, one of his many cash infusions. Her high school classmates, who she hadn’t been in close touch with in decades, fundraised by selling grilled chicken, rice and beans from a roadside tent. Two GoFundMe fundraisers raised nearly $30,000 and Banda rented her late sister’s house while putting her own in forbearance. But months of insecurity takes its own, sleepless toll. She needed to sell some internet services to catch up. After sticking the Spectrum Wi-Fi flyers onto empty storefronts, she drove to pick up her kids from school. The following day she had a morning meeting at a barbershop for what would be her first sale back at work. Turning on Trump and voting Democratic for the first time A lifelong Christian, Banda had voted her anti-abortion stance in past elections. When her sister was kidnapped and murdered by her ex-husband in 2020, Banda retreated from religion. The cancer brought her back to church with an apology to God, but it also made her rethink her politics. She voted for Trump in 2016, and his first four years seemed steady, so she voted for him again in 2020. Democratic President Joe Biden's tenure, including the tail end of a global pandemic and rising inflation, felt like bedlam, so she voted for Trump to return to the White House in 2024. But two years later and fighting an expensive disease, she had found no respite from high prices. So when James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminary student running for U.S. Senate as a Democrat, visited one of Banda’s fundraisers — speaking about his diabetes and his work in the Texas Statehouse to lower the price of insulin — it moved her. “Imagine if he can do that for the cancer,” she said. Talarico and his Republican opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, have different approaches to healthcare. Talarico wants all Americans to be able to join Medicare; Paxton proposed a $25,000 tax deduction for out-of-pocket medical expenses. Talarico also supports a law guaranteeing abortion access nationwide, which Banda has voted against for years. But after she slid into debt to stay alive, after her grocery bills mounted and the high school had to comp the kids' soccer gear she couldn't afford, Banda’s anti-abortion concerns have been superseded by costs. “Because it’s what I’m living,” she said. “I'm living it." Banda cast an early ballot for Talarico. “Never voted Democrat before today!!” she wrote in a text with blue heart emoji. Her news will come on Election Day, in a doctor's office Banda had just started a new cancer-targeting medication that cost $16,000 a month, reduced to $500 by insurance. By the afternoon, she was nauseous and fatigued, unable to eat. The malaise would keep her home the next day. She would miss the meeting with the barbershop to close her first deal since getting sick, though she felt confident it was in the bag. But Banda pushed through the discomfort one evening to join her family as they replaced the flowers at her sister's tomb. She drove past the headstones and oak trees in the evening’s slanting light, and the family gathered around Melissa Banda's tomb in an open-air mausoleum. There was no speech. Their eulogy was her father, Fidel Banda, methodically clipping and arranging the flowers for his daughter. Banda walked along the wall of tombs. She will find out on Election Day whether the cancer is in remission or whether it's spread to her organs. “This one’s for me,” she said, pointing to a blank tomb next to her sister's. “Mom!” said her daughter with the huffiness of a 9-year-old. “Why would you say that?” Banda smiled and added, “in a hundred years." This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/she-voted-trump-every-time-123400184.html

articles.title: Inflation under Trump is only about half the rate under Biden. Voters are still just as mad.
articles.summary: So far in President Trump's second term, prices in the US have risen only about half as quickly compared to his predecessor's four years in office. Yet Trump has a 72% disapproval rating on the issue and risks paying a steep political price — just as former President Joe Biden did — with voters drawing a direct connection between rising prices and the president's policies. In the last election cycle, prices of all items rose more than 20% during Biden's term , sparking widespread voter angst. This time around, price growth is notably slower, rising 5.4% in a little less than two years since Inauguration Day. But a Yahoo Finance analysis of price data shows that a few major outliers have hit Americans' wallets in an outsized way, largely due to increases in goods affected by the war in Iran and tariffs. Fuel oil and gasoline are perhaps the most dramatic examples, spiking over 30% beginning in March in response to the war in Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz. And voters have noticed, as evidenced in poll after poll. A New York Times/Siena poll released this week found 73% of likely voters disapprove of the president's handling of gas prices. Trump underscored the salience of energy prices when he posted a charge this week that "Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election." Trump has often pushed back against questions about high energy prices, saying they won't be a problem once the Iran war ends. Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries Link between price spikes and Trump policies The connection between price increases and Trump's tariff policy has also been in evidence. Coffee prices have risen nearly 23% during Trump's second term (more than double the rate under Biden) as tariffs raised prices before Trump scrapped many of the coffee duties late last year in response to coffee drinkers' unhappiness. Goods like toys and footwear have likewise risen rapidly as importers from China and elsewhere in Asia faced new tariffs. Toys are a particularly stark example, falling by 4.6% during Biden's term and then rising by 7.8% so far in Trump's term. "Maybe the children will have two dolls instead of 30 dolls, and maybe the two dolls will cost a couple of bucks more than they would normally," Trump said in a rare acknowledgment of tariff-fueled price increases when he was pressed on the issue in April. Other goods have moved in the opposite direction. Eggs jumped by an average of 2.57% each month when Biden was in the White House, but have dropped 3.82% each month of Trump's term so far, the analysis shows. But tariffs remain in focus and unpopular, with an average of polls from the Silver Bulletin finding that 62.7% of Americans disapprove of how Trump has handled trade and tariffs versus 32.8% who approve. President Donald Trump is seen after a rally on October 22 in Sioux City, Iowa.. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images Gas in focus in the final weeks of the campaign Despite the different roots, inflation has emerged as the central political problem for Trump and his party — as it was for Biden and Democrats — and comes as early voting is already underway for the Nov. 3 midterms. And perhaps no individual price tag is more politically charged, for any president, than the cost of a gallon of gas. Trump is trying to make his case as gas prices are averaging about $4.30 per gallon and diesel is elevated after setting an all-time price record last month, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). Trump has taken multiple actions just this week to try to rein in prices, including $8 billion in support for farmers and invoking the Defense Production Act on Thursday to direct new funds to increase refining capacity. Yahoo Finance Trump touted the moves before voters in Iowa on Thursday , saying the release of $150 million would lead to more production of diesel and gasoline. Yet he faces the inconvenient fact that his record on gas prices is now all but indistinguishable from Biden's. Since Jan. 20, 2025, prices have averaged $3.449 per gallon according to data from the Energy Information Administration . Under Biden, the average price was $3.455 per gallon over his four years. Trump spent much of the last campaign promising the opposite, pledging $ 2 per gallon gasoline and vanishing inflation in nearly every 2024 campaign speech. That is leading voters to blame the president for the state of affairs. This week's national poll from the New York Times and Siena University found that 75% of voters view economic conditions as only fair or poor, and a solid majority put the blame on Trump. As Ipsos also put it this week in a summary of recent findings :  "Americans' confidence in the economy has been bad since the Iran war began [and] now the bottom has dropped out." Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. articles.title: 价格打折，哪些股票超跌了？
articles.summary: 双十一，股市也开启了“打折促销”。近期市场快速调整，创业板指从4372点回落到2700点以下，科创综指来到1300附近。不少前期热门股票大幅回撤，以历史高点为参照，中际旭创、新易盛、东山精密等热门股价格已跌至约四折。 尽管10月23日市场明显反弹，但科技成长板块此前的调整幅度已经不小，也引发了市场对科技股是否会重演周期股大幅波动的担忧。 股票毕竟不是普通商品，价格打折不等于估值便宜。 从交易层面看，下跌太快，股价反而可能出现反弹。但这类交易性反弹，并不是我们要讨论的“超跌”。 我们所说“超跌”是基于完整盈利周期基础上的估值便宜。 投资者在这个价格上购买股票，可能会输掉一些时间，但不会丧失本金。 为此，我们拿出光伏，锂电的龙头，跟光通信龙头进行比较。光伏和锂电都有完整的周期可以参考。 通过选取隆基绿能、宁德时代和中际旭创作为典型案例，比较不同景气阶段下的盈利和估值变化，观察经历大幅调整后，当前股价是否已经出现估值超跌。 看PE、PB的历史分位，不能判断估值 股价大幅调整后，市场通常把PE、PB放到历史的维度里去比较 ：当前低于历史多少分位，就说股票有多便宜。 例如，仅看原始PE的分布，宁德时代截至今年9月30日，15.85倍的pe低于此前五年20个季度的全部观测值；中际旭创当前32倍估值处于历史40%分位水平。单看历史估值，宁德时代似乎已经比较便宜，中际旭创也不算贵。 但问题是，这一估值背后所对应的盈利并不相同。 对于景气波动较大的公司，历史估值分位未必能反映真实的估值水平。仅是用历史分位，很难判断在周期中，是否真的“超跌”。 行业景气高低点，企业盈利水平差异明显 周期股在景气高点和低谷的盈利差异往往很大。即期估值容易受到利润波动的影响。 把三家公司利润放在一起来进行对比，通过年末EPS和ROE的观察，对周期差异就有更直观的感觉。 隆基2022年末ROE还有23.8%，2026年二季度却降至-15.5%，EPS也转为负数；中际旭创2021年末ROE只有7.6%，2026年二季度已超过51%，EPS从约1元增至13.4元；宁德时代的EPS则从2021年末约4.3元增加到2026年二季度约17.1元。 景气高点，利润增长会压低PE；景气低谷，利润收缩甚至亏损，又会使PE大幅抬升或失去参考意义。这就是单看即期PE容易踩的“坑”。 因此，仅凭PE、PB的历史分位，难以准确判断股价是否超跌。 我们尝试以历史稳态ROE为基准，还原企业在正常盈利水平下的估值，进一步观察当前股价是否具备安全边际。 估值是否合理，需要考虑完整的景气周期 经历大幅调整后， 优质公司的股价是否已经跌至具有吸引力的位置，需要从完整的行业景气周期出发，以正常盈利水平为参照。 我们采用历史ROE中位数作为稳态盈利水平，据此测算修正后的EPS和PE，观察企业在正常盈利能力下的历史估值区间，进而判断当前股价是否具备估值安全边际。 三家公司，三个答案 我们以三家公司各自的盈利周期起始日为起点，选取此后26个季度的ROE（TTM）中位数作为稳态盈利参考，并据此修正历史EPS和PE。 这样剔除不同景气阶段盈利波动对PE的影响，在相对统一的盈利水平下，观察市场过去给予企业的估值是否合理。 隆基绿能：便宜的前提，是先把利润赚回来 隆基的历史样本为2016Q1—2022Q2。26个季度的ROE中位数为19.53%，对应的标准化PE中位数为26.43倍。 问题是，隆基目前仍在亏损，负PE已经没法正常比较。按2026Q3的11.21元股价倒推：如果未来ROE恢复到约7.22%，对应PE为26.43倍；如果恢复到历史中位数19.53%，对应PE约9.76倍。 对隆基来说，能不能恢复盈利、能恢复到什么水平，比股价跌了多少更重要。 宁德时代：把盈利调回常态后，估值仍偏低 宁德的历史样本为2018Q2—2024Q3。ROE中位数为13.48%，标准化PE中位数为49.12倍，历史25%—75%区间为36.79—81.43倍。 2026Q3，宁德时代PE为15.85倍。把当期ROE折回13.48%后，修正PE约26.64倍，仍低于历史区间下沿，处在历史约3.8%分位。 换句话说，宁德的低PE并不只是当下盈利较高造成的。即使用历史中位数ROE来算，估值相对过去仍然偏低，具备一定的历史估值吸引力。 中际旭创：PE不高，不代表安全垫已经很厚 中际的历史样本为2020Q1—2026Q2。ROE中位数为10.73%，标准化PE中位数为61.95倍。 只看当前32倍PE，它处在原始PE历史约34.6%分位，处于较低分位水平。但如果用历史ROE中位数来折算，当前示意标准化PE约153倍，处于历史约84.6%分位，超过历史中间50%区间。 两种口径之所以差这么多，关键在于对高ROE能持续多久的判断。 如果未来ROE逐渐回到历史水平，当前价格在这套模型下没有明显的绝对吸引力；但如果AI光模块需求带来的高盈利能维持较长时间，用10.73%的历史ROE做假设又可能过于保守。 跌下来以后，究竟怎样才算便宜？ 三家公司给出了不同的答案：宁德时代在盈利还原至历史中枢后，估值仍处于历史较低分位；隆基绿能的估值吸引力取决于盈利修复；中际旭创则需要关注当前高ROE的持续性。 从跨周期估值角度看，判断股价是否超跌，不能仅依据股价回撤幅度或短期交易性反弹，更需要考察企业在稳态盈利水平下的估值位置。 若盈利回归常态后，估值仍明显偏高，说明当前价格对盈利回落的风险反映可能不足；若在相对保守的盈利假设下，估值仍处于历史低位，则可能具备一定的安全边际，但仍需结合基本面判断折价是否合理。 不过需要注意的是，历史中位数不能代替未来盈利预测，行业景气和公司竞争力也可能发生变化。但把价格与可持续的赚钱能力放在一起看，至少能避免把“跌得多”直接当成“够便宜”。 股价打了几折不重要。重要的是，利润回到正常水平以后，价格是否依然合理。 本文来源： 东吴证券陈李、葛晓媛 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: AI势头回落并非牛熊分界
articles.summary: AI趋势回落并非熊市开端，非AI可能反而会面临更为有利的环境 1）产业趋势回落≠牛转熊。A股在过往存在比较广泛的“产业趋势回落=牛转熊”的思维，核心是过往的产业趋势（2006~2007年的工业与金融、2009年的地产与基建、2013~2015年的移动互联、2019~2021年的能源转型等）对其他经济部门带来广泛的拉动作用。而本轮AI产业的进展，至少在短期内对其他经济部门产生了不少挤出效应，包括导致了物料和资源价格暴涨、推动了债券市场供需紧张和长债利率大幅飙升、一定程度上挤出就业，财富效应的增长极为失衡，市场分化的程度历史罕见，甚至出现了所谓“硅基世界”和“碳基世界”的对立。这也意味着，过往“产业趋势行情结束=牛转熊”的经验可能并不适用于这轮AI硬件主导的行情，非AI的不少板块早已步入下行趋势，而AI只不过最后“补跌”。 2）AI短期内对其他部门产生了负外部性，若AI势头回落，一些非AI板块反而可能有转机。目前已经显性化的负外部性至少包含三类：第一，电子元器件、电力等基础生活物资的大幅涨价，抬高生产和生活成本，压抑其他领域需求，典型的如消费电子；第二，算力基础设施投建推动私人部门巨额债务融资，推升全球无风险利率，对所有高利率敏感性的需求产生冲击；第三，挤出就业，尤其是对于年轻人就业的影响，比如根据斯坦福与ADP就业数据库今年9月最新数据，自动化型AI使用占比最高职业组的22~25岁就业较2022年11月下降10.9%，最低组同期上升7.8%。这些因素引发了实体经济和市场的剧烈分化，但反过来看，如果AI投资的速度在未来有所放缓，非AI板块可能也不会面临如此负面的宏观环境，比如无风险利率出现大幅回落。事实上，从当前的美债定价来看，10年期美债利率的走向与北美AI硬件股的股价走势高度相关，如果未来出现持续性的回落，至少对海外的非AI部门需求可能产生促进。 估值收缩的进程今年已基本完成，行情宽度有望逐步拓展 1）AI的二阶导修正、非AI的估值收缩，都有望在今年基本完成。AI完成了第一波“二阶导”修正。与2021年底至2022年4月底的新能源行情调整类似，本轮AI同样是在产业景气仍在、增速预期转弱时提前下修估值。从估值收缩的视角出发，本轮AI硬件的估值压缩幅度已与2022年新能源第一轮调整相当。根据Wind数据，7月1日以来，电子与通信板块整体法PE（TTM）从74.0倍压缩至42.4倍，降幅42.8%；2022年新能源第一轮调整（2021年12月17日-2022年4月26日），电力设备及新能源板块市值下PE从51.2倍压缩至27.8倍，降幅45.7%。站在全球对比的视角下，A股非AI板块处于全球估值洼地。我们用中、美、日、韩四个市场的AI与非AI龙头篮子，以整体法测算PE（TTM）并进行跨市场对比。截至10月22日，A股是唯一一个AI相对非AI估值溢价仍高于历史中枢的市场：AI/非AI的PE倍数为4.4倍，处于2016年以来82%的分位，美、日、韩的这一倍数则分别回落至1%、17%、24%的分位。美、日非AI非金融龙头的PE分别为33.5倍和23.0倍，处于98%和95%的分位；A股非AI非金融龙头只有15.6倍，处于历史21%分位，消费、制造、医药龙头分别只处于12%、1%、3%的分位。当然，低估值源于疲弱的内需以及市场对非AI领域外需的潜在担忧（贸易摩擦、海外高利率、高油价等），有其合理性。但换个角度看，这种导致低估值的悲观，很大程度上源于今年的现实与年初市场期待的巨大割裂，投资者难以预料在“十五五”的第一年广义财政赤字会意外转为大幅负增长、市场从美联储降息预期转为加息预期、10年期美债利率创了2007年以来新高、中欧贸易摩擦突然升温、美伊战争爆发且持续快一年。这种落差，是导致不少非AI板块在今年业绩增长亮眼的情况下估值发生剧烈收缩的原因。当下，至少市场已经充分认知到了这些宏观负面因素，无论是海外利率还是国内政策，任何边际上超预期的变化可能都有助于改变当下A股相对于全球市场更为悲观的估值体系。 2）K型分化逐步收敛，行情宽度有望逐步拓展。对于AI侧，商业化空间增长焦虑还将继续约束AI投资单年度的绝对规模体量，同时加深市场对于未来“一阶导”拐点的警惕，AI对于非AI板块的虹吸很难再出现，同时考虑到主流机构资金仍然超配TMT板块，市场反弹过程中的持仓均衡化过程也将制约AI板块的弹性。我们看到，在本周市场止跌企稳的过程中，率先反弹的AI新技术是筹码出清相当彻底且机构持仓比例低的机器人板块，而非算力基建相关的板块。对非AI板块，当下几乎所有的负面因素都已经被市场所认知（即便可能并未完全定价），在经历一轮系统性调整后，低预期本身就是有利的条件。以出海板块为例，中欧贸易摩擦已经摆在台面上，未来每年的规则修订谈判和博弈可能是常态化的，企业最终还是会凭借强大的竞争优势适应；人民币在明年只要升值速度有所放缓，汇兑损失就会同比减少，就会带来净利润率的回升；美国中期选举后民主党如果控制国会，中东战争格局可能会有积极变化，所带来的油价影响可能边际上转弱；AI投资增速放缓，带来海外长端无风险利率回落，对非AI行业的需求抑制作用减弱。由于这些负面因素在今年已经被投资者系统性认知，只要后续有边际上的好转，对非AI板块本身也产生促进。 资金面的出清需要时间，PB-ROE 代表的稳健回报型策略可能更加占优 资金面快速恶化的过程大概率已接近尾声，在本周ETF明显放量的信号下，主动买盘开始谨慎流入市场，融资盘去杠杆的负向循环被阻断。截至10月21日，两市融资余额已回落至2.45万亿元，相对年内高点累计减少5600亿元，降幅18.6%，已回到去年11月下旬的水平，交易层面的降温更为明显，融资买入额占两市成交额的比例（MA5，下同）6月平均为9.86%，7月降至8.99%，9月为8.66%，10月以来进一步降至8.01%，10月16日读数7.84%，为2024年9月以来的最低值，低于“9.24”行情前约9%的水平。活跃私募的仓位同样回到低位，对中信证券渠道调研显示，样本活跃私募仓位8月7日当周以来持续回落，10月16日已降至67.5%，为2024年3月以来最低，较76.3%的历史中位数低8.8个百分点。虽然资金面指标已经回落到较低的位置，但彻底出清并开始持续改善仍然需要时间，这个阶段动量和景气策略会持续弱势，市场轮动速度加快，而以PB-ROE外代表的低估值质量型策略会更占优。目前有两类行业在明年满足这样的框架，一类是具备高股息率和稳健盈利增速的品种，如白电、纺织服装、食品调味、火电等，另一类是带有供给出清潜力逻辑的品种，如油运、快递物流、头部地产开发商、部分锂电材料、石化偏中游的环节等。 articles.title: SemiAnalysis创始人深度解析：AI投资还能撑多久？英伟达护城河还能守住吗？内存荒何时结束？
articles.summary: AI基础设施投资仍有增长空间，但融资成本上升、半导体供应链受限与自研芯片竞争加剧，正在共同考验这轮AI热潮的持续性。 在10月23日于美国举行的CASPA第35届年度大会上，SemiAnalysis创始人兼CEO Dylan Patel、Bernstein董事总经理兼高级分析师 Stacy Rasgon，以及Austin Lyons围绕半导体行业前景展开讨论，重点涉及AI基础设施投资、供应链瓶颈与芯片竞争格局。 Patel指出， 当前AI算力需求依然旺盛，但基板、内存等关键环节的产能约束，正在限制基础设施扩张。 与此同时，融资成本大幅攀升，缺乏长期客户订单的新兴云服务商越来越难以获得资金，AI投资能否持续推进，不仅取决于需求，也取决于项目的融资能力与回报。 对于英伟达，Rasgon认为，其产品性能提升仍能支撑较高售价，但云厂商自研芯片正在改变竞争格局。 随着Google TPU、亚马逊Trainium以及OpenAI等企业的自研芯片计划推进，英伟达即使继续增长，也可能面临市场份额和定价能力的双重压力。 内存市场则面临另一重考验：HBM需求旺盛、行业利润率处于高位，但厂商扩产可能在2028年后逐步改变供需关系。未来两年，融资能力、关键零部件供给与自研芯片的竞争，将成为影响AI基础设施扩张速度和产业链利润分配的关键变量。 华尔街见闻总结要点如下： AI投资仍有增长空间，但融资成本正成为重要约束。 美国10年期国债收益率突破5%，部分新兴云服务商无担保债券收益率接近15%。缺乏长期客户订单的企业融资难度更大，项目建设节奏将越来越取决于融资能力与投资回报。 半导体供应链瓶颈短期难解，基板与内存是关键制约。 基板、HBM、光学互联组件及洁净室产能均面临供应限制。相比之下，电力短缺可通过现场发电等方式部分缓解，半导体供应链扩产则需要更长时间。 内存短缺可能延续至新增产能释放，2028年后供需格局面临转折。 HBM需求旺盛，内存行业毛利率据称已达88%—90%；但如果新增产能在2028年后集中投产，而需求增速放缓，内存价格与利润率可能承压。 英伟达仍有性能优势，但自研芯片正在挑战其定价权。 英伟达持续通过性能提升支撑高售价，但Google
